facts.title: feat: render a commit without a pull request next to the pull requests
facts.description:
Closes #257

- **Why:** a commit that belongs to no merged pull request was left out whenever the release had one. A fix pushed straight to `main` shipped with the release and appeared nowhere, and nothing said so. The decision to render such commits, with its reasons, is recorded in #257.
- **A direct commit becomes a change of its own**, as a release without pull requests already did: subject as title, no description, no labels. The same rules follow, so a `chore:` or `ci:` push is dropped as `Internal`, and `labels.onlyIncludeLabeled` drops it for having no labels.
- **Membership comes from `PullRequestInfo.CommitShas`**, which the reader fills from the request per commit it already makes. No extra GitHub request. It is read from every merged pull request, not only the ones left after revert pairing, so the commits of a reverted pull request do not come back as direct pushes.
- **A merge commit without a pull request is skipped:** what it brings in is the merged commits, which are in the range themselves. `git log` now reads the parents (`%P`), and `CommitInfo.IsMerge` carries it. A release without pull requests skips its merge commits too, instead of rendering "Merge branch ..." as `Other`.
- **Range order:** a pull request stands where its first commit is, a direct commit where it is. A release of pull requests alone keeps exactly the order it had.
- **The run says what happened:** the summary's `Release:` line adds `3 commits without one (1 merge commit, skipped)` when there are any, and the run record's `release` gets `commitsWithoutPullRequest` and `mergeCommitsSkipped`. Both are new fields, so the run record stays at schema version 3. `changelog.json` is unchanged: commit-based changes are already part of it.
- **Docs:** `what-goes-into-a-release.md` describes the behavior, including that a direct revert pairs nothing. `run-metrics.md` and `run-record.md` describe the new counts.

**Reproduced and verified end to end, no network, no tokens:** the built binary in a scratch repository: `v0.1.0`, then a pull request's commit on a branch, `fix: crash on start` pushed to `main`, a local `--no-ff` merge, `v0.2.0`. GitHub and the model are a local stub that knows the one pull request.

```
Before:  Release:  3 commits, 1 pull request, 1 fact (1 with a description, 12 characters)
After:   Release:  3 commits, 1 pull request, 2 commits without one (1 merge commit, skipped), 2 facts (1 with a description, 12 characters)
```

What the model received after the fix:

```
- [1] Feature: feat: add search - Adds search.
- [2] Fix: fix: crash on start
```

Tests: `ReleaseChangeResolverTests` (a direct commit next to a pull request in range order, merge skipped; a reverted pull request's commits stay out; a release without pull requests skips merges; `DirectCommits` counts skipped merges), `GitCliCommitReaderTests` (a real two-parent merge is `IsMerge`), `RunReportFormatterTests` and `RunRecordJsonSerializerTests` (the new counts). Test pull requests that stand next to commits now name their commits, as the reader does. Full suite 858 passing, build without warnings, `dotnet format` clean.

facts.title: fix(cli): add the trailing slash to a GitHub API URL written without one
facts.description:
Closes #272

- **Why:** `Chartula__GitHub__ApiBaseUrl` worked only with a trailing slash. The adapters request relative paths (`repos/...`), and relative resolution replaces the last segment of a base without one, so `.../api/v3` sent every request to `.../api/repos/...` and the run failed with a `404` that read like a missing repository or token.
- **Added, not required:** GitHub's own documentation writes an Enterprise URL without the slash, so asking for it would keep the trap and only improve the message. `ReadOptions` appends it once, after the URL passed `EndpointUrl.Require`.
- **In `ReadOptions`, not in `Create`:** the header line reads the same options, so it shows the URL the requests actually go to, `https://github.example.com/api/v3/`, whichever form was set.
- The "Keep the trailing slash" paragraph in `docs/github.md` is gone, and the example uses the form without the slash (roadmap follow-up 2.3, the #272 part).

**Reproduced and verified end to end** against a local HTTP stub that logs the request path (`http` is accepted for `127.0.0.1`), `preview --tag v0.1.0-preview.3`:

```
Chartula__GitHub__ApiBaseUrl=http://127.0.0.1:18765/api/v3
  main:         GET /api/repos/goldbarth/chartula/commits/7620e6d.../pulls
  this branch:  GET /api/v3/repos/goldbarth/chartula/commits/7620e6d.../pulls
                GitHub: http://127.0.0.1:18765/api/v3/, token from GITHUB_TOKEN
Chartula__GitHub__ApiBaseUrl=http://127.0.0.1:18765/api/v3/
  both:         GET /api/v3/repos/goldbarth/chartula/commits/7620e6d.../pulls
```

Tests: `GitHubHttpClientFactoryTests` (both forms resolve a request to the same URL, and the options carry the slashed form the header shows). Full suite passing, build without warnings, `dotnet format` clean.

facts.title: fix(config): read an empty excludeCategories list as dropping no category
facts.description:
Closes #277

- **Why:** `filter.excludeCategories: []` is meant to drop no category, and was read as no setting, so the default `[Internal]` stayed in force. `ChangeFilterRules` and `FilterOptions` both document that an empty list replaces the default; the file never got that far.
- **Two places lost it, not one:** `Flatten` turned an empty sequence into no key, as the issue says. Behind it, `ChartulaConfiguration.Build` layers the settings with `AddConfiguration`, whose provider passes an empty value on as no value. A unit test on `Flatten` alone passed while the run still kept `[Internal]`; the end-to-end run below found the second one.
- **An empty list is read as the value `[]`:** the YAML spelling of an empty list, and a value the layering keeps. Rebuilding the layering to keep empty values instead would change what an empty `Chartula__` variable means today (no setting), for every key.
- **Only `excludeCategories` reads it:** the binder leaves an empty list `null`, and this is the one list whose default differs from empty. `categories.order: []` already falls back to the default order in `CategorySettings`, and the `labels.*` lists default to empty. Both were checked with `[]` in the run below.
- **Honored, not refused:** the issue allowed either. Keeping internal work is a legitimate choice, and without `[]` there is no way to express it.
- `Chartula__Filter__ExcludeCategories=[]` works the same way, for a run without a list in the file.
- `docs/configuration.md` states the behavior (roadmap follow-up 2.7, the #277 part).

**Reproduced and verified end to end**, `preview --tag v0.1.0-preview.3 --audience technical`, model pointed at a closed port so no token is spent. The range holds 7 pull requests, one of them `build:` (Internal):

```
default                                  7 pull requests, 6 facts
excludeCategories: [], on main           7 pull requests, 6 facts
excludeCategories: [], this branch       7 pull requests, 7 facts
  plus order: [] and labels.internal: [] 7 pull requests, 7 facts
Chartula__Filter__ExcludeCategories=[]   7 pull requests, 7 facts
excludeCategories: [Documentation]       7 pull requests, 5 facts
```

Tests: `FilterWiringTests` (no list and `excludeCategories:` keep the default, `[]` in the file and in the environment drops nothing, a list replaces the default), built through `ChartulaConfiguration.Build` so the layering is covered; `ChartulaYamlConfigurationTests.An_empty_list_is_kept_as_a_value_of_its_own`. Full suite passing, build without warnings, `dotnet format` clean.

facts.title: fix(cli): report an answer the SDK cannot read as unreadable, not as unreachable
facts.description:
Closes #263

- **Why:** a model call whose answer the SDK could not read was reported as an endpoint that could not be reached. `Describe` took every failure without an HTTP error response for "no answer at all", so a local Ollama that sent a `finish_reason` the OpenAI SDK does not know sent the user looking for a network problem.
- **The transport decides, not the exception type:** `ModelErrorResponseHandler` already saw every response of a model call and kept only the errors. It now keeps the last response of either kind. A call that fails after a success response got an answer; one with no response at all did not. Each SDK throws its own type on an unreadable body, and this holds for both without naming one.
- **The last response wins:** after a retried error, an answer replaces the error, since it is the response the SDK gave up on.
- **The message names the answer and what could not be read:** `answered 200 OK for model '...', but the answer could not be read: Unknown ChatFinishReason value 'weird_reason'.` An SDK that meets an unknown value puts it after the parameter name on a line of its own; the message names the value instead. Any other failure keeps the SDK's message, on one line. A second line says the endpoint is reachable and its answer is not in the form the SDK expects.
- **"Could not be reached" stays** for failures where no response arrived, with the transport's own reason, as before.

**Reproduced and verified end to end, no network, no tokens:** the built binary in a scratch repository with two tags, GitHub and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint both served by a local stub that answers `finish_reason: "weird_reason"`.

Before:

```
$ chartula preview --tag v0.2.0 --repo o/n --audience technical
  (failed) Changelog generation for 'v0.2.0' failed: openai-compatible at http://localhost:8791/v1 could not be reached for model 'granite': Unknown ChatFinishReason value. (Parameter 'value')
           Actual value was weird_reason.
```

After:

```
  (failed) Changelog generation for 'v0.2.0' failed: openai-compatible at http://localhost:8791/v1/chat/completions answered 200 OK for model 'granite', but the answer could not be read: Unknown ChatFinishReason value 'weird_reason'.
           The endpoint is reachable, but its answer is not in the form the provider's SDK expects.
```

Tests: `ModelCallFailureTests` through the real SDKs with a stubbed network: an unknown `finish_reason` is reported as unreadable with its value, an answer that is not JSON is unreadable and not unreachable for both providers, an answer after a retried error replaces it, and the existing unreachable test still gets "could not be reached". Full suite 856 passing, build without warnings, `dotnet format` clean.

facts.title: fix(config): refuse chartula.yaml and chartula.yml side by side
facts.description:
Closes #278

- **Why:** with both `chartula.yaml` and `chartula.yml` in the directory, a run read `chartula.yaml` and ignored `chartula.yml` without a word. A user editing the `.yml` file saw none of their settings take effect.
- **Refused, not resolved:** two files are the same ambiguity as a key the file may not set, one level up. Whichever file won, the other's settings would not be in force, so the run stops instead of choosing.
- **The message names both full paths and the fix:** keep one, move the wanted settings into it, delete the other. It goes through the existing `Configuration error:` path, before any GitHub request or model call.
- `docs/configuration.md` "Where the file is read from" states the behavior (roadmap follow-up 2.7, the #278 part).

**Reproduced and verified end to end**, binary from this branch, a scratch clone with the repository's `chartula.yaml` (`model: claude-sonnet-5`) and a `chartula.yml` with `model: model-from-yml`:

Before, on `main`, the `.yml` file is ignored:

```
Model:  anthropic at its default endpoint, key from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
        claude-sonnet-5, thinking provider-default
```

After:

```
Configuration error: Both /.../repro/chartula.yaml and /.../repro/chartula.yml exist, and a run reads one configuration file. Keep one: move the settings you want into it and delete the other.
```

Exit 1. A single `chartula.yml` is still read as before (`The_file_is_named_as_it_was_found`).

Tests: `MalformedYamlTests.Both_file_names_present_is_refused_naming_both_paths`. Full suite passing, build without warnings, `dotnet format` clean.

facts.title: fix(pipeline): check that the token may publish before the first model call
facts.description:
Closes #262

- **Why:** `generate` found out that the token could not publish only in its last step, after every model call. A read-only token, or none, paid for the whole run and then ended on `Not published:`.
- **The check is `POST releases/generate-notes`:** GitHub requires Contents write for it and stores nothing, so it answers "may this token write releases?" without writing one. It costs one GitHub request. The answer is discarded.
- **Port, not a pipeline detail:** `IReleaseNotesWriter.EnsureCanWriteAsync` sits next to `WriteAsync`, so the platform decides how to ask, and `chartula doctor` (#254) can reuse the same check.
- **Only `generate` checks:** `preview` and `generate --no-publish` publish nothing, so they do not ask and still run without a token.
- **After the range confirmation, before the pull requests are read:** the confirmation stays ahead of the first API request, as #282 set it up, and a refused token stops the run before the per-commit requests and the model calls.
- **Same message as a refused publication, worded as a check:** `GitHub does not let this run publish ...` instead of `GitHub refused to publish ...`, since nothing was sent. The pipeline adds that the run stopped before any model call and names `--no-publish`.
- **The late failure path stays:** GitHub can still refuse the write for a reason the check cannot see, and the run then keeps the written files and reports `Not published:` as before.
- `docs/github.md` and `docs/cli.md` describe the check (roadmap follow-up 2.3, the #262 part).

**Reproduced and verified end to end** against `goldbarth/chartula` `v0.1.0-preview.3`, `GITHUB_TOKEN` unset, local Ollama (`qwen3:14b-ctx24k`), `--audience technical`, in a scratch clone:

Before, on `main`:

```
Not published: the release notes.
  GitHub refused to publish the release notes for v0.1.0-preview.3 to goldbarth/chartula (401 Unauthorized).
    The request carried no token: GITHUB_TOKEN is not set.
    Publishing needs a token with Contents read and write on goldbarth/chartula.
  ...
  Total:            8,889 tokens in 7.1 s
```

After, on this branch:

```
Range:  the commits after v0.1.0-preview.2, up to v0.1.0-preview.3 (7 commits)
Error: GitHub does not let this run publish the release notes for v0.1.0-preview.3 to goldbarth/chartula (401 Unauthorized).
  The request carried no token: GITHUB_TOKEN is not set.
  Publishing needs a token with Contents read and write on goldbarth/chartula.
  The run stopped before any model call. --no-publish writes the files without publishing them.
```

Exit 1, no run record, no file written. The same run with `--no-publish` renders and writes as before.
The endpoint itself, checked with `curl`: `200` with a token that can write, `401` without a token, `404` with a token on a repository it cannot write to. A tag GitHub does not know still answers `200`.

Tests: `ReleasePipelineTests` (a refused check stops before rendering and writing, `preview` and `--no-publish` do not check, `generate` checks once and publishes), `GitHubReleaseNotesWriterTests` (a token that may write, one that may not with the permission GitHub names, no token). Full suite passing, build without warnings, `dotnet format` clean.

facts.title: feat(cli): print the installed version with chartula --version
facts.description:
Closes #255

- **Why:** a user had no command to find the installed version. `chartula --version` printed `Unknown command '--version'.` and exited with 1, and the version showed up only after a run, as `toolVersion` in `changelog.json`. The bug report and the alpha feedback form ask for it.
- **`chartula --version` prints the informational version:** `chartula 0.1.0-preview.3+<commit>`, exit 0, on stdout. It is the text `changelog.json` records as `toolVersion`, so a report and a run file name the same build, and a build from source is told apart from a release.
- **Checked before anything else is read:** no checkout, no configuration, no key and no token are needed, so it works from any directory and right after install.
- **Only `--version`:** no `-v` or `version` word. A short flag is easy to add later, and hard to take back once a script depends on it.
- **The help text lists it**, and `docs/cli.md` mirrors the help line for line and says what the output is.
- **The issue templates ask for its output**, and `docs/install.md` tells the user to check an install with it, instead of `--help`. The install scripts still smoke-test with `--help`, since `CHARTULA_VERSION` can pin a release that has no `--version`.

**Verified with the built binary, from an empty directory:**

```
$ chartula --version; echo $?
chartula 0.1.0-preview.3+953a939f0b2fb99c0834790b8363a057e0da18da
0
```

Tests: `VersionTests` runs the built CLI with `--version` and no key or token, and checks the output, exit 0 and an empty stderr; the help text names it. Full suite 854 passing, build without warnings, `dotnet format` clean.

facts.title: fix(cli): say that --no-publish writes every file and skips only the release notes
facts.description:
Closes #256

- **Why:** the help text said `--no-publish` writes `changelog.json` and `CHANGELOG.md`. It also writes `release-<tag>.md` and the run record; only the GitHub release notes are left out. The documentation will point to `chartula --help` for the options, so the line has to be right.
- **The line names the exception, not the files:** `Write every file, but publish no GitHub release notes.` A list of files goes stale with the next output, and `--audience` already says which outputs an audience leaves out.
- **`docs/cli.md`** mirrors the help text line for line, and its `--no-publish` section now names the run record next to the three files.

**Verified with the built binary:**

```
$ chartula --help | grep no-publish
  --no-publish   Write every file, but publish no GitHub release notes.
```

facts.title: feat: render a first tag from the first commit, and confirm a large range before it is read
facts.description:
Closes #281

- **Why:** a first tag was refused, and the expected range, every commit up to the tag, had to be switched on with `--whole-history`, whose only effect was to lift the refusal. The name and the message called that range "the whole history", although it ends at the tag, so the message read as the opposite of what the run does.
- **A first tag starts at the first commit:** the same default one step earlier than the previous tag, with no flag. `--whole-history` and `WholeHistoryException` are gone; `CommitRange.IsWholeHistory` is `StartsAtFirstCommit`. A run that still passes `--whole-history` is not broken silently: the CLI ignores unknown options, and the run stops at the question below.
- **The protection stays, as a question:** a first tag, or a range with more commits than `range.confirmAboveCommits` (default 200), is confirmed before any GitHub request or model call. The text names the range with both ends, what it costs (one GitHub request per commit, every pull request to the model once per audience) and `--since <ref>` as the way to start later.
- **Twice, no by default:** `Render all N commits up to <tag>? [y/N]`, then `Continue? [y/N]`. Anything but `y` stops with `Stopped: ...`, exit code 1, nothing spent.
- **Without a terminal the run stops, and `--yes` confirms up front:** a CI job has nobody to answer, and an unattended run should not spend on a range nobody approved. `docs/ci.md` advises passing it for that one release, not for good.
- **The threshold also covers a range between two tags:** otherwise a forgotten `--since` on a long history is caught only on a first tag. 200 is well above a release of a few dozen pull requests merged with merge commits, and well below GitHub's 5,000 authenticated requests an hour. An unreadable or negative value is refused, since falling back to the default would let a range run unasked.
- **Rule in the domain, question in the CLI:** `LargeRangeRule` decides, `IReleaseRangeGate` is the port, `ConsoleRangeGate` asks. It writes to stderr, so a prompt stays out of a changelog redirected from stdout, and asks only when stdin is a terminal. Without a gate the pipeline counts a range as declined.
- **The run header names every range**, not only large ones: `Range:  the commits after v1.2.0, up to v1.3.0 (7 commits)`.
- **Run record schema version 3:** `range.start: "whole-history"` is `"first-commit"`. A value changes its name, which the stability rule counts as breaking. `changelog.json` is unchanged.

**Verified end to end, no network, no tokens:** binary from this branch in a scratch repository with three commits, `v0.1.0`, and one commit after the tag:

```
$ chartula preview --tag v0.1.0 --repo o/n < /dev/null
Range:  every commit up to v0.1.0 (3 commits), the first tag
        It costs 3 GitHub requests, and every pull request in it goes to the model once per audience.
        To start later, pass --since <ref>: the commits after <ref>, up to v0.1.0.
        No terminal to confirm this. Pass --yes to confirm it up front.
Stopped: The range of v0.1.0 was not confirmed, so nothing was read from GitHub or sent to the model.

$ chartula preview --tag v0.1.0 --repo o/n          # in a terminal, answering y, then n
Render all 3 commits up to v0.1.0? [y/N] y
This sends every pull request in the range to the model. Continue? [y/N] n
Stopped: The range of v0.1.0 was not confirmed, so nothing was read from GitHub or sent to the model.

$ Chartula__GitHub__ApiBaseUrl=https://127.0.0.1:1/ chartula preview --tag v0.1.0 --repo o/n --yes < /dev/null
Range:  every commit up to v0.1.0 (3 commits), the first tag
Error: Could not reach the GitHub API for commit bc6e833...: Connection refused (127.0.0.1:1)
```

The count is 3, not 4: the commit after the tag is not in the range. `docs/cli.md` matches `chartula --help` line for line.

Tests: `LargeRangeTests` (declined and ungated first tag stop before GitHub and the model, confirmed and `--yes` render, above and at the threshold, a named start is not asked about), `ConsoleRangeGateTests` (header with both ends, two yeses, anything else declines, no second question after a no, no terminal names `--yes`), `RangeWiringTests` (default, configured, refused values), `FirstTagTests` (built CLI without a terminal stops, with `--yes` goes on to GitHub), `ShallowCloneTests` (`--yes` does not get past a shallow clone), run record `first-commit` and version 3. Full suite 852 passing, build without warnings, `dotnet format` clean.

facts.title: docs: turn the README into a landing page
facts.description:
Follows #269, #270, #271, #273, #274, #275 and #276, which gave every topic the README carried a page of its own.

- **Why:** the README was the manual: install details, every CLI option, the credentials table, the outputs, a cost table and the configuration all lived there, next to the pitch. A newcomer had to scroll through reference material to find out what Chartula is and how to try it, and every fact the README repeated had a second place to go stale.
- **A landing page, in this order:** the pitch, the real example from Ingestor `v3.2.0`, what it promises and what it does not, the status, a quick start, one line per provider, the known limitations, and the documentation index.
- **Quick start:** install, a model key and a GitHub token, `cd`, `preview`, `generate`. One sentence each on what a reader trips over first: `preview` costs what `generate` costs, `chartula-runs/` belongs in `.gitignore`, and a first tag asks where the release starts. The token line says `generate` needs it to create the draft, rather than suggesting a small public release can do without.
- **Providers in four lines:** Anthropic, OpenAI, a hosted compatible endpoint and a local server, with a link to the recipes. The `qwen3:8b` example goes with the credentials table, since `docs/providers.md` recommends no local model.
- **Known limitations stay here, and only here.**
- **The index is grouped by audience:** setting it up, understanding the output, reference, and working on Chartula. Versioning and the roadmap join it.

facts.title: docs: add a guide to writing pull requests for Chartula
facts.description:
Follows #274, whose rules this guide turns into advice for authors.

- **Why:** a team adopting Chartula has to decide what to ask of its pull request authors, and nothing said what each piece of input changes in the output. `what-goes-into-a-release.md` describes the rules; this page answers "what should we write, and what do we get for it".
- **Levels, not a checklist:** what Chartula delivers without any convention, the minimum (a Conventional Commits prefix), what pays off (`!` or `BREAKING CHANGE`, two sentences of description, `closes #N`), and what is optional (visibility and action labels). Each level shows its effect on the output.
- **The minimum carries a table** of where `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `chore` and a title without a prefix land in the technical and customer notes, and the consequence: without the prefix, a `Rewrite comments for readability` change reaches customers.
- **A title check for CI without a third-party action:** a `grep` on the title with the types Chartula knows, read through `env` so a title cannot inject shell code. A typo in the type fails the check instead of turning the change into `Other`. The check requires a space after the colon, which Chartula itself does not.
- **The description level quotes a real entry:** the technical entry for #251 from `v0.1.0-preview.3`, whose details come from its description, not its title. It repeats the warning that the description is published with `changelog.json`.
- **`closes #N` is stated at its actual worth:** an issue number in `linkedIssues` at `title-description-and-issues`; the renderings do not link issues.
- The README index gets a row.

**Verified:** the grouping table matches `GroundedFactsFactory.cs` (technical: Added, Fixed, Changed; customer: What needs action, What's New, What's Changed, Bug Fixes) and `RenderingComposer.cs` (`**Breaking:**`). The title regex was run against nine titles, including `wip`, `Fix(cli)!: ...` and a title without a space after the colon. The workflow parses as YAML, and every relative link and anchor resolves.

facts.title: docs: explain what goes into a release in docs/what-goes-into-a-release.md
facts.description:
Follows #273 and #266. Updated when #257 (direct pushes dropped) and #258 (`title-description-and-issues` reads no issue) close.

- **Why:** what a release contains was split across `cli.md` (the range, a shallow clone, reverts) and `configuration.md` (visibility), and the rest was not written down: which prefixes map to which category, what makes a change breaking, the order the filters apply in, and which audience a change reaches. A user could not predict from the docs why a change appeared, or did not.
- **One page, in the order Chartula decides:** the range, pull requests or commits, reverts, the category, breaking status, what is dropped, who can meet a change, and how much of it the model reads.
- **Every prefix as a table** (`ConventionalCommitCategorizer.cs`), with the consequence: a repository without Conventional Commits gets every change as `Other` and none of its internal work filtered.
- **The filter order** (`ChangeFilter.cs`, `LabelRulePolicy.cs`): an exclude label, then `onlyIncludeLabeled`, then breaking changes kept, then excluded categories. A commit carries no labels, so `onlyIncludeLabeled` keeps nothing of a release that falls back to commits.
- **Which audience a change reaches, as a table** (`GroundedFactsFactory.cs`): an `internal` label narrows the customer rendering only, and a change that reaches no rendering is still a fact in `changelog.json`.
- **Revert rules completed from `RevertPairing.cs`:** which titles count as a revert, `Reverts #N`, a revert that is itself reverted, and no pairing when the release falls back to commits.
- **Current behavior stated with its issue:** direct pushes are left out once a release has a merged pull request (#257); issue numbers are extracted from the text, and no issue is read (#258).
- **Moved, not repeated:** `cli.md` keeps the `--since` and `--whole-history` table and links here; `configuration.md` `labels` keeps its key table and links here. The README index gets a row.

**Verified:** each rule checked against `ReleaseChangeResolver.cs`, `PullRequestBody.cs`, `RevertPairing.cs`, `ConventionalCommitCategorizer.cs`, `ChangeFilter.cs`, `LabelRulePolicy.cs`, `FactBaseBuilder.cs` and `GroundedFactsFactory.cs`. Every relative link and anchor resolves.

facts.title: docs: add a complete GitHub Actions job in docs/ci.md
facts.description:
Follows #271 and #269, whose token permissions and install settings the job uses.

- **Why:** the README CI section showed one `actions/checkout` snippet. Everything else a CI job needs was left to the reader: installing a pinned version, passing the keys, the token permissions, where the written files go, and what happens to the draft.
- **A complete job to copy:** triggered by a `v*` tag, full history (`fetch-depth: 0`), a pinned Chartula installed with the install script of that same release, secrets as environment variables, `permissions` of `contents: write` and `pull-requests: read`, and an artifact with every file the run writes.
- **Each step carries its reason and its consequence:** a pinned version keeps a new release from changing the notes unannounced; without `contents: write` the model calls are paid before GitHub refuses; without the artifact the files vanish with the runner.
- **`--tag` and `--repo` go through `env`,** not straight into `run`, so a tag name cannot inject shell code.
- **What happens to the draft:** publishing it, the published-release case from #249, and why `CHANGELOG.md` is committed through a pull request rather than by the job (the tag's checkout is not a branch). `--no-publish` with `contents: read` for a job that should leave GitHub alone.
- **Another provider:** the step for OpenAI, with the model in `chartula.yaml` and only the endpoint and key in the job.
- **Alpine container:** git goes in before the checkout, since `actions/checkout` fetches files without history when git is missing; `libstdc++`, `curl` and `ca-certificates` for the musl binary.
- The README CI section becomes a sentence and a link, and the index gets a row.

**Verified in Docker, no tokens spent:** the job's steps in `ubuntu:24.04` and `alpine:latest`: full clone, pinned install from the tag's `install.sh`, then `chartula preview --tag v0.1.0-preview.3 --repo goldbarth/chartula` with a dummy key. Both read 7 commits and 7 pull requests from GitHub; Ubuntu ends on the expected `401` at the first model call. The workflow parses as YAML, and every relative link and anchor resolves.

**Not verified:** a run inside GitHub Actions itself (`$GITHUB_PATH`, the built-in token's `permissions`, the artifact upload).

facts.title: docs: move GitHub access to docs/github.md
facts.description:
Follows #270 and #266. Updated when #262 closes, since the section on a read-only token describes the late check it fixes.

- **Why:** everything about GitHub access was spread over the README credentials, the `cli.md` environment section and `configuration.md` `github`, and the rate limit was written out in all three. A user setting up a token had to read three pages, and a correction had to be made three times.
- **One page, one home:** the token and its permissions, the rate limit, GitHub Enterprise, private repositories, and what `generate` writes to GitHub. `cli.md`, `configuration.md` and the README keep one sentence each and link here.
- **Permissions as a table per command:** `preview` and `generate --no-publish` need read-only, `generate` needs Contents read and write. A read-only token cannot change the repository, so the page recommends it until publishing.
- **Private repositories:** the message a run prints when its first request is refused, and why GitHub answers `404` rather than `403`, so the typo and the missing token are both named.
- **The rate limit** moves here unchanged from #266, including the merge-commit consequence and the ten-and-sixty example, plus the few requests `generate` adds for the release notes.
- **GitHub Enterprise:** `Chartula__GitHub__ApiBaseUrl` with the header line that confirms it. The page says to keep the trailing slash: without it, the relative request paths replace the last segment, so `https://ghe.example.com/api/v3` sends requests to `/api/repos/...` and every request fails with `404`. The fix in code is #272.
- **What `generate` writes:** a draft for a tag without a release, replaced notes for an existing one (#249), the re-run that finds its earlier draft, and publishing a draft with `gh release edit --draft=false`.
- **A read-only token on `generate`:** the files are written and the model calls paid for before GitHub refuses; the page shows that output and recommends `--no-publish` until #262 moves the check.
- `cli.md` keeps a pointer that all three credential variables can be renamed, which the removed token section used to carry.

**Verified:** the messages are taken from `GitHubPullRequestReader.cs`, `GitHubReleaseNotesWriter.cs`, `GitHubErrorResponse.cs` and `ReleaseCommand.cs`. The trailing-slash behavior follows from `GitHubHttpClientFactory` setting `BaseAddress` and the adapters requesting relative paths; checked with RFC 3986 resolution of `repos/...` against both forms of the URL. facts.title: docs: move installing to docs/install.md
facts.description:
Follows #268, which set the platform count to eight. First of the new end-user pages; updated when #255 (`chartula --version`) closes, so "Update" can say how to check the installed version.

facts.title: docs: correct the changelog.json fields and show a real example
facts.description:
Follows #266. Updated again when #260 settles the role of the file.

- **Why:** `docs/changelog-json.md` is the contract downstream consumers build on, and four of its field descriptions did not match the code. A consumer that trusts `title` to be the pull request title, or `linkedIssues` to come from GitHub's issue links, builds on something the file does not hold.
- **Consumers:** the widget and the RSS feed are gone (#32 and #33 are parked). The page names what reads the file today: a tool that reacts to a release, such as a webhook.
- **The current release only:** every `generate` run overwrites the file, by design. One file is one release notification, so a consumer that receives it needs nothing else and has nothing to tell apart from earlier releases.
- **A warning on `description`:** it carries each pull request description in full, so publishing the file publishes all of them, including notes written for reviewers.
- **`title` corrected** (`ReleaseChangeResolver.cs`): the trimmed title, or, when it says nothing (empty, `Merge ...`, or exactly `wip`, `update`, `fix`, ...), the first informative line of the description, then `PR #<n>`. The fallback reads the description whatever `factBase.depth` says, so a title of `fix` shows a line of the description even at `title-only`. A commit-based change carries its subject.
- **`linkedIssues` corrected** (`FactBaseBuilder.cs`): the numbers after `close`, `fix` or `resolve` in any form and a `#`, in the title or description. No issue is read.
- **`renderings`:** Markdown, only the audiences the run rendered, and at least one in any written file, because a run in which no audience rendered writes nothing (`ReleasePipeline.cs`).
- **`description`:** `null` for a commit-based change, which the table did not say.
- "the file is meant to be published" becomes "the file may be published", so the page does not answer #260 ahead of time.
- **A real example:** three of the six changes of Chartula's own `v0.1.0-preview.3`, with the renderings and provenance its run wrote. #246 shows a fact that no rendering carries. The page says what was cut: descriptions after their first line, and the entries of the other three changes.

**Verified:** each field description checked against `ChangelogDocument.cs`, `ReleaseChangeResolver.cs`, `FactBaseBuilder.cs` and `ReleasePipeline.cs`. The example parses as JSON and is taken from the run's `changelog.json`, trimmed but not rewritten.

facts.title: docs: correct GitHub requests, the cost of preview, and what publishing replaces
facts.description:
Follows #265, and is stacked on it: the base is `docs/provider-status`, so this diff shows only this change. GitHub retargets it to `main` once #265 is merged.

- **Why:** four statements about a run's contact with GitHub did not match the code, and each one leads a user to a wrong decision: running without a token for a release that exhausts the limit, running `preview` to save tokens, and expecting a draft where a published release is changed in public.
- **One request per commit, not per pull request** (README credentials, `docs/cli.md` environment, `docs/configuration.md` `github`). `GitHubPullRequestReader` asks `commits/{sha}/pulls` for every commit of the range, and the range comes from `git log` without `--no-merges`. A pull request merged with a merge commit therefore costs one request for the merge commit and one for each commit on its branch. The README carries the example: ten squash-merged pull requests take ten requests, ten of five commits each take sixty, the whole unauthenticated hour.
- **The rate limit is named:** the claim that an exhausted limit fails with a 403 naming a commit is gone. `GitHubErrorResponse.DescribeCredentials` recognizes the limit and says so; `docs/cli.md` shows that message.
- **`preview` costs what `generate` costs:** both run the same pipeline and make the same model calls, so "to check token cost before committing to a real run" is removed and the cost is stated instead.
- **An existing release is not a draft:** `GitHubReleaseNotesWriter` creates a draft only when the tag has no release, and otherwise patches the body alone. "Nothing goes public until you publish it on GitHub" is replaced by that, and the replaced notes of a published release join the known limitations with a link to #249.
- **GitHub is the only source:** a known limitation says Chartula reads pull requests from GitHub or GitHub Enterprise only, and the GitLab CI snippet is gone. `docs/cli.md` still names GitLab CI where it quotes the shallow-clone error, because that is the message `GitCliCommitReader` prints.

**Left for its own change:** the warning a run starts with when no token is set (`GitHubTokenNotice.cs`) still says "roughly one per pull request", as does a comment in `LlmServiceCollectionExtensions.cs`. That is code, not documentation.

**Verified:** `git grep` finds no "per pull request" request count, no "names a commit", and no "goes public" left in the README or `docs/`. The branch merges into `main` without a conflict.
